claims.text: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state are governed by intrinsically low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction permits easy dislocation glide in the as-cast alloy.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi contains few or no nanoscale precipitates.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi contains few or no short-range-ordered regions.
The absence of nanoscale precipitates or short-range order leaves few effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
The lack of effective dislocation obstacles keeps work hardening low.
The lack of effective dislocation obstacles keeps yield strength and hardness low.
A controlled aging treatment can induce nanoscale precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Aging-induced nanoscale precipitates act as dislocation-pinning points.
Precipitate pinning increases resistance to dislocation motion.
Aged samples will have higher hardness than the as-cast baseline.
Aged samples will have higher tensile yield strength than the as-cast baseline.
The applicable starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in an unaged, single-phase solid-solution state.
The alloy composition remains equimolar before and after aging.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to ambient-temperature testing at moderate strain rates.
The comparison excludes aging conditions that cause significant grain coarsening.
The comparison requires the aged material not to enter a multiphase regime.

contradictions.description: The intervention is intended to form nanoscale precipitates, which ordinarily constitute a distinct phase, while the boundary simultaneously requires the material to remain single-phase and prohibits entry into a multiphase regime.

The hypothesis distinguishes intrinsic lattice friction from extrinsic precipitate pinning, but the falsification rule equates absence of pinning points with low lattice friction. The proposed aging comparison directly tests precipitate strengthening, not the claimed intrinsic lattice-friction origin of the starting strength.
